apparatus.basis: Standard Lyc. ⲟⲩⲉⲉ = ⲟⲩⲁ 'one'; with ⲛⲟⲩⲱⲧ 'alone' forms standard Coptic 'one alone' construction. Trace of ⲉ̣ visible.
Word ⲧⲟⲩⲃⲟ 'purification' continues from line 1 ⲧⲟ̄|; ⲛⲧⲟ restored gives ⲧⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲩⲃⲟ 'the purification' as object of ⲁⲍⲱⲅⲣⲁⲫⲉ 'depict.'
ⲁⲍⲱⲅⲣⲁⲫⲉ ⲙⲙⲁⲥ idiom: 'depict her/it' with 3sg.f object suffix ⲙⲙⲁⲥ referring back to ⲧⲙⲉⲥⲟⲧⲏⲥ 'the mediation' (fem.). ⲙⲙⲁ restored at line start.
Greek loan ⲕⲁⲑⲁⲣⲓⲍⲉ < καθαρίζειν 'purify' continues from line 3 ⲛⲥⲉ-; standard editor's restoration.
Demonstrative ⲡⲓ- begins ⲡⲓⲕⲁⲧⲏⲭⲟⲩⲙⲉⲛⲟⲥ 'this catechumen' (line 5). Bracket on transcription marks ⲡⲓ as restored at line-end.
ⲧⲱⲧ in series with ⲁϩⲡⲉⲓⲑⲉ 'he was persuaded' and ⲁϩⲕⲁⲣⲱϩ 'he became silent' — three sequential verbs of acquiescence. ⲧⲱⲧ ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧ 'be persuaded/agreed' is the standard idiom.
ⲙ̄ⲙ̄ⲁⲥ = ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲥ '(saying) it' — the ϫⲱ ⲙⲙⲟⲥ idiom for direct discourse. Editor's standard restoration.
Greek loan αἰσθάνεσθαι 'perceive,' Lyc. ⲣ̄- + ⲁⲥⲑⲁⲛⲉ; 2sg present ⲧⲣ̄- (= ⲕⲣ̄-). Parallel to preceding ⲧⲥⲁⲩⲛⲉ 'you know.' Editor restores ⲧⲣ̄ⲁ at start.

notes.decision: Decorative chapter marker centered above page body, indicating a new chapter begins on this page (lines 7-10 chapter heading). Translated 'The Chapter' preserving the standalone Greek loanword.

Marginal sigil appearing on lines 7 and 9 (twice on line 9). Likely the chapter number — Coptic numerals ⲯⲅ̄ = 703, which does not match a chapter number directly, but in Manichaean codices marginal sigils like this often indicate chapter or section markers. Tentatively rendered '[ch. 93]' (taking ⲯⲅ̄ as a possible scribal/dialectal form of 93) but the precise reference is uncertain. The triple repetition at line 7 and flanking line 9 is consistent with the Polotsky convention of placing chapter sigils in margins for visual prominence.

ⲡⲉⲧⲉ ⲙⲛ̄ ⲃⲁⲙ + infinitive = standard Coptic impersonal 'that which there-is-no power to (do).' ⲙⲙⲁⲥ is 3sg.f object referring back to ⲧⲙⲉⲥⲟⲧⲏⲥ 'the mediation' (fem.). The catechumen's purification cannot be visually depicted because catechumens are not purified all in one place but dispersed.

Tentative parsing as ⲭⲁⲕ ⲙⲉϩ 'fully complete' or as a verb of fulfillment + ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧ 'in heart' = 'fulfilled in heart.' Could alternatively be ⲭⲱⲕ-ⲙ̄ⲙⲁϩ 'complete (themselves).' The sense is that catechumens, lacking unified purification, also lack inward completion of heart.

Reading ⲉⲛ as the Lyc. negative particle: 'shall it not become Sin?' (rhetorical question implying anxiety that good acts may turn to sin). ⲛⲁⲙⲁⲍ tentatively parsed as future + a 'become/fill' verb. The catechumen worries that his offering, though intended as a good (ⲁⲅⲁⲑⲟⲛ), may inadvertently strike the principle of mercy (turning into Sin against the living soul).

The cosmic injury-doublet: ⲟⲩⲱⲃⲁ 'stripe' (per glossary) + Greek πληγή 'blow.' Recurs at lines 14, 29, 33 — the central conceptual figure of the chapter, representing the harm an offering at the wrong moment may inflict upon mercy (or the living soul).

ⲧⲗⲃⲟ = 'heal, restore' (cf. accumulated ⲡⲗⲅⲟ/ⲧⲗⲅⲟ 'healing'). The Apostle's response: the catechumen's offering is not Sin but healing — what is done in mercy on the day of offering aims to restore mercy itself, bringing it unto Life and Rest.
Standard parable-introducer 'For this matter is likened to two men.' ⲧⲛⲧⲁⲛⲧ̄ qualitative of ⲧⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲛ 'be likened.' Begins the parable of the two men struck by an enemy that follows.

Tentatively read as a verbal form related to ⲱϣⲃⲁ 'wound' (cognate with ⲟⲩⲱⲃⲁ 'stripe' in line 14, 29) — 'they have wounded him.' Could alternatively be ⲟⲩⲱϣⲃ̄ 'answer' (ⲣ̄- + ⲟⲩⲱϣⲃ̄), but the wound-context of the surrounding parable strongly favors the injury-reading.
Negative imperative ⲙ̄ⲡⲱⲣ + ⲣ̄- (verbalizer) + ⲍⲁⲧⲉ (Lyc. = ϩⲟⲧⲉ 'fear') = 'do not fear.' The Apostle's reassuring opening to the catechumen.
